# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-40 (Extended v251)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to autumn Year 10, and 1814-1820 (Marseilles/Pharaon timeline). Key Paris locations: Rue Plumet, Place de la Bastille, Prison Charlemagne, Rue de l'Homme Armé No. 6, Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Champs-Élysées, Rue Saint-Honoré, Luxembourg Garden, Quai aux Fleurs, Rue du Temple, sewers (Sainte-Avoye, Louvre, Montmartre, belt, Amelot, Beautreillis), Marais, Blancs-Manteaux, Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine, Rue de l'Écharpe, Rue Pavée, Rue des Trois-Pavillons, Saint-Paul church, Rue Beautreillis near Arsenal, Grand Sewer, Rue de l'Hôpital, Père-Lachaise cemetery, Rue Mondétour, Tuileries, Rue Saint-Jacques, Rue de la Jussienne, Rue Coq-Héron, Rue Bussy, Lyons, Grenoble. English locations: Kelmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Dungate, Ravenmere, Staveford, Wilwick, Salcombe, Wilholt, Torton, Yarlby, Gagny, Lagny, Gulhaven, Quenford, Dunby. Marseilles: La Canebière, Rue de Noailles, Allées de Meilhan, Rue du Grand Cours, Rue de l'Homme Armé, Medusa fountain, Palais de Justice, Accoules clock-tower, Rue Caisserie, Rue Saint-Laurent, Rue Taramis, La Consigne, Frioul, Pilon, Porto-Ferrajo, Naples, Elba, Island of Elba, Point des Catalans, Ile Ratonneau, Rue de la Loge, Catalans, Madrid, Cape Pharo, Cape de Morgiou, Château d'If, San Pierdarena vineyard, Palatine Hill. Rome locations: History of City of Rome, Palace archives. Islands: Island of Monte Cristo (deserted rock, conical form, twenty-five miles from Pianosa, between Corsica and Elba), Tiboulen, Lemaire, Planier lighthouse, Pomègue, Daume. **Timeline: 1814-1820 Marseilles; 1 March 1814 Dantès' arrest; spring/summer Year 10 English subplot; autumn Year 10 English subplot; winter Year 10 current time.**

## English Subplot Summary (through Chapter 40, winter Year 10)

**Established solemn promises**: Semor swore to Isric Thornmere to rebuild wall at Kelmere (summer Year 9). Elra gave Matho promise to plant orchard above Gulhaven; Pelia gave Fenelle promise to plant orchard above Salcombe (summer Year 7); Movie swore to Nerine promise to plant orchard above Wilholt (autumn Year 7); Yera Haskick swore to Nerine Prydenridge to repair chapel roof at Kelmere (winter Year 8); Kassa Stenson kept promise to Taric Corrley: wall at Yarlby rebuilt by harvest; Kassa's husband swore to rebuild wall at Ostcombe. Yera Haskick gave Lurald Stenworth solemn promise to carry sealed letter to Quenford (winter Year 9). Eldest daughter of Lura Haskick kept promise: chapel roof repair at Kelmere completed by harvest (winter Year 9). Fewyn gave Havus Stenworth solemn promise to carry sealed letter to Salcombe (winter Year 9). Luena gave husband of Yera Stenworth solemn promise to pay old debt owed to Haskick family (winter Year 9). Sebin swore to youngest daughter of Havus Stenworth to repair roof of chapel at Wilholt (spring Year 10). Harine swore to wife of Sebin Brackick to teach children of Kelmere their letters (summer Year 10). Fenelle Lindmere swore to Rorald Lindmere to plant orchard on slope above Salcombe, shook on it (autumn Year 10).

**Chapter 34-35 migrations**: Taric Corrley moved from Dungate to Kelmere with Kassa Stenson. Luena Stenenridge's only son moved from Ostcombe to Elmhaven. Pelde Stenworth married Sebin Brackick at Torton; couple lived in Torton. Fewyn Stenworth moved from Gulhaven to Yarlby with Havus. Pelia Lindmere moved to Yarlby with Rorald Lindmere. Havie Prydenridge found work in Staveford, moved there; Isric Thornmere followed within the month. Youngest daughter of Fewyn Stenworth became herbalist. Youngest son of Nelan Brackick became weaver.

**Summer Year 10 births and changes**: Ismira Stenson died from festering wound; bone compass went to Matho Stenson. Son Brevus Brackick born to Luvie Prydenridge and Semor Brackick; family lived in Ostcombe. Daughter Elvie Brackick born to Pelde Stenworth and Sebin Brackick; family lived in Torton. Son Madan Prydenridge born to Wenelle Lindmere and Rovus Prydenridge; family lived in Kelmere. Febin Prydenridge moved from Kelmere to Elmhaven. Davus became mason. Daughter Kamira Stenenridge born to Movie Prydenridge and Thizek Stenenridge; family lived in Elmhaven.

**Chapter 38-39 autumn movements and events**: Ilrald Prydenridge left Torton, settled in Wilwick. Dalis left Torton, settled in Yarlby. Harine went to Wilwick. Jotho Thornmere quit Ostcombe, took lodgings in Quenford. Yera Stenworth followed him to Quenford within the month. Havie Prydenridge found work in Dunby, moved there, did not return to Staveford. Isric Thornmere went along to live in Dunby as well. Peten Haskick rode out of Quenford; by next market day was living in Gulhaven. Lura went along to live in Gulhaven as well. In chapel at Yarlby, Dalis Stenworth married Movus Brackick; couple lived in Yarlby (autumn Year 10). RUMOR—Isric Thornmere told Havie Prydenridge old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar. RUMOR—In burned letter, youngest son of Malis Prydenridge revealed old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar. **Late one night Kassa Brackick confided to Davus that Stenenridge mill ledger was rewritten after flood.** **Late one night Kassa Brackick told Jotho Thornmere that Stenenridge mill ledger was rewritten after flood.**

**Chapter 40 autumn/winter scenes and events**: Dantès escaping Château d'If at seven o'clock. Frost silvered hedges overnight. Rain threatened since morning but held off. Bell for vespers rang thinly across roofs. Children chased hoop down lane, shrieking. Wind off water smelled of salt and tar. Cart loaded with turnips creaked past well. Bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage. Dog barked at nothing and went quiet. Road all ruts and puddles after thaw. "You look tired," Kassa told Volan Stenworth, who did not deny it. **Kassa Brackick argued with carter over price of sack of oats.** Someone chalked crooked sun on wall of forge. Smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields. **In Yarlby: Pelia Lindmere and Rorald Lindmere talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse. Rorald Lindmere spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight. Pelia walked long way round to avoid muddy square. Pelia watched clouds and predicted rain, wrongly. Pelia Lindmere read almanac aloud, mispronouncing half the saints.** Baker's boy was late again, line at oven grew long. **Winter of tenth year; hill farms of Staveford.**

**Deaths**: Marald Corrford died from fall from mill loft at Ravenmere; laid in churchyard at Ravenmere.

**New events**: Parcel from Matho Stenson reached Luvie Prydenridge containing bone compass, now hers to keep. Parcel from Lura Haskick reached Bremira Corrford containing silver chalice; Bremira's to keep.

## Marseilles/Pharaon Subplot (1814-1820): Dantès' Escape from Château d'If

**Edmond Dantès' arrest (1 March 1814)**: Young sailor jumped into skiff at La Canebière. Reported Captain Leclere dead; would become captain with M. Morrel's aid. Wedding feast at La Réserve with Mercédès; betrothal announced. Danglars and Fernand conspired; Danglars wrote denunciation with left hand naming Dantès as Murat's agent. Magistrate arrested Dantès during feast. Villefort interrogated Dantès about commission to deliver letter in Paris to Noirtier (Villefort's father). **Villefort destroyed fatal letter—only proof against Dantès. Dantès was doomed.** Villefort reported conspiracy to King Louis XVIII, received Legion of Honor cross. Noirtier disguised himself: cut whiskers, changed cravat, wore dark brown coat, narrow-brimmed hat, walked past sentries with bamboo switch.

**Dantès' imprisonment (1 March 1814–Chapter 39)**: Boarded boat to Frioul; reached Château d'If. Locked in bare underground chamber; marked plaster daily. Expected release in fortnight; waited nearly four years. Governor transferred; Edmond became number 34. At end of second year ceased marking time. Sustained by pride, then doubt, then supplication. **Resolved: "I wish to die." Chose starvation. Heard mysterious scratching—subterranean workman mining way.**

**Abbé Faria revealed (Chapter 38)**: **Following night Dantès found head: small stature man, hair blanched by suffering, deep-set penetrating eye, long black beard, thin furrowed face, sixty or sixty-five years. Identified as: "I am Abbé Faria, imprisoned since 1811; previously confined three years in Fenestrelle fortress. In 1811 transferred to Piedmont. Learned Napoleon had son named king of Rome."** **Faria imprisoned because in 1807 he dreamed plan Napoleon realized in 1811; sought one large empire instead of petty Italian principalities. Plan will never succeed; Italy fated to misfortune. "I am poor mad prisoner of Château d'If."**

**Faria's education and escape plan (Chapters 38-39)**: **Possessed five thousand volumes in Rome library; found one hundred fifty well-chosen books possess all man needs. Recites Thucydides, Xenophon, Plutarch, Titus Livius, Tacitus, Strada, Jornandes, Dante, Montaigne, Shakespeare, Spinoza, Machiavelli, Bossuet. Made vocabulary; knows one thousand words. Made excellent pens from whiting-head cartilages. Wrote _A Treatise on Possibility of General Monarchy in Italy_—sixty-eight weeks; tore up two shirts and handkerchiefs for pages; wrote with own blood for important notes; dissolved soot in Sunday wine for ink.** **Dantès possessed prodigious memory, astonishing quickness of conception, mathematical turn of mind. Already knew Italian and little Romaic; at end of six months spoke Spanish, English, and German.** **Over fifteen months, miners began labors with only tools: chisel, knife, wooden lever. Fresh earth thrown out window; rubbish pulverized so finely wind carried it far away. At end of fifteen months level finished, excavation completed beneath gallery. Two workmen heard measured tread of sentinel overhead. Propped flagstone with small beam from walls. Rope ladder of cords twenty-five to thirty feet concealed behind fitting stone at bed's head.**

**Faria's death and Dantès' substitution (Chapter 39)**: **Faria seized with cataleptic illness identical to attack one year before imprisonment. Instructed Dantès: draw out one of bed's feet, find small phial half-filled with red-looking fluid. When catalepsy reached height, force open teeth with knife, pour eight to ten drops of liquor down throat. Fit lasted two hours; Dantès administered appointed number of drops; hour passed; consciousness returned. Faria fully regained but helpless and exhausted: "Third attack will either carry me off, or leave me paralyzed for life." Urged Dantès to escape alone.** **One night Edmond awoke hearing plaintive voice calling from Faria's dungeon. Faria seized with catalepsy symptoms. Warned silence necessary. Urged Dantès: "you will appear like an angel of salvation" to next prisoner; Dantès "will no longer have half a dead body tied to you as a drag." Told Dantès: "Providence has done something for you... it was time I should die." Blessed Dantès as "sole consolation of my wretched existence." In dying moment, revealed: "The treasure of the Spadas exists... Hasten to Monte Cristo—avail yourself of the fortune—for you have indeed suffered long enough."** **Dantès administered twelve drops, waited. No change. Applied phial to Faria's purple lips, poured entire remaining liquid down throat. Half hour, hour, hour and a half elapsed. Body gradually grew cold; heart's pulsation became deep and dull, then stopped. Face became livid; eyes remained open, glazed.** **Dantès executed bold substitution: opened canvas sack containing Faria's corpse; drew corpse from sack and bore it through tunnel to his own chamber; laid it on his couch; tied around its head the rag he wore at night; covered it with counterpane; kissed the ice-cold brow; tried vainly to close resisting eyes; turned head toward wall; entered tunnel again; drew bed against wall; returned to Faria's cell; took needle and thread; flung off his rags; got inside sack; placed himself in posture corpse had lain; sewed up mouth of sack from inside.**

**Dantès' escape (Chapter 40)**: **Seven o'clock, jailer brought supper. Grave-diggers came to seek him. Deposited supposed corpse on bier. Edmond stiffened himself to play dead man. Party, lighted by man with torch, ascended stairs. Edmond felt fresh and sharp night air; mistral was blowing. Sensation in which pleasure and pain were strangely mingled. Felt himself flung into air like wounded bird, falling with rapidity that made blood curdle. With horrible splash, darted like arrow into ice-cold water, uttering shrill cry stifled by immersion beneath waves. Although stunned and almost suffocated, held breath. Right hand held knife open; rapidly ripped up sack, extricated arm, then body; despite all efforts to free himself from shot, felt it dragging him down. Bent body and by desperate effort severed cord binding legs, moment when seemed actually strangled. With mighty leap rose to surface of sea; shot dragged down to depths sack that had nearly become his shroud. Waited only to get breath, then dived to avoid being seen. Arose second time fifty paces from where first sunk. Saw overhead black and tempestuous sky; wind driving clouds occasionally suffering twinkling star to appear; before him vast expanse of waters, sombre and terrible, whose waves foamed and roared as if before approach of storm. Behind him, blacker than sea and sky, rose phantom-like vast stone structure, projecting crags like arms extended to seize prey; on highest rock was torch lighting two figures. Fancied these forms were looking at sea; doubtless strange grave-diggers had heard his cry. Dived again, remained long time beneath water. Easy feat to him; usually attracted crowd of spectators in bay before lighthouse at Marseilles when swam there; unanimously declared best swimmer in port. When came up again, light had disappeared.** **Ratonneau and Pomègue inhabited, as was islet of Daume. Tiboulen and Lemaire safest for Dantès' venture. Islands of Tiboulen and Lemaire a league from Château d'If. Saw light of Planier gleaming like star. By leaving light on right, kept Island of Tiboulen little on left. Swam toward Tiboulen. Faria's words rang in ears beneath waves; hastened to cleave way through them. Found with pleasure captivity taken away nothing of his power; still master of element on whose bosom he had often sported as boy.** **Fear relentless pursuer clogged Dantès' efforts. Listened for any sound audible; every time rose to top of wave scanned horizon, strove to penetrate darkness. Fancied every wave behind him was pursuing boat; redoubled exertions, increasing rapidly his distance from château, exhausting his strength. Swam on still; already terrible château had disappeared in darkness. Could not see it but _felt_ its presence.** **Suddenly sky seemed to him become still darker and more dense; heavy clouds swept down towards him; at same time felt sharp pain in knee. Fancied moment that shot him; listened for report; heard nothing. Put out hand, encountered obstacle; with another stroke knew had gained shore. Before him rose grotesque mass of rocks, resembled vast fire petrified at moment of most fervent combustion. It was Island of Tiboulen. Dantès rose, advanced few steps, with fervent prayer of gratitude, stretched himself on granite, which seemed softer than down. Then, in spite of wind and rain, fell into deep, sweet sleep of utter exhaustion. At expiration of hour Edmond awakened by roar of thunder. Tempest let loose, beating atmosphere with mighty wings; from time to time flash of lightning stretched across heavens like fiery serpent, lighting up clouds that rolled on in vast chaotic waves.**
